items.readable_text:
Content:
A linear equation in the variables [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] is an equation that involves just these two variables, possibly with some constants. There should be no powers on any of the variables and the variables can't be multiplied together.

Content:
For example, the following are linear equations:

Content:
[MATH: y = x + 4, \qquad
y = -3x, \qquad
5y = 6x,\qquad
2x + 3y = 9]

Content:
On the other hand, the following are not linear equations:

Content:
[MATH: y = x^2 - 2x, \qquad
y^2 = - 4x + 2, \qquad
y = 2xy]

Content:
A solution of a linear equation is an ordered pair [MATH: (x,y)] that makes the equation true.

Content:
For instance, the ordered pair [MATH: (3, 7)] is a solution to the equation [MATH: y = 3x - 2] because if we replace [MATH: x] with [MATH: 3] and [MATH: y] with [MATH: 7,] we get

Content:
[MATH: y|= 3x − 2; (7)|= 3(3) − 2; 7|= 9 − 2; 7|= 7✓]

Content:
The above is a true statement, so [MATH: (3, 7)] is a solution to the equation [MATH: y = 3x - 2.]

Content:
Important: A linear equation in two variables has an infinite number of solutions, not just one!

sections.normalized_html:
The plotted points correspond to the [MATH: xy]-pairs [MATH: A(-1, 3)] and [MATH: B(2,-4).] To check whether each point is a solution to the equation, we substitute it into the equation and see if it results in a true statement.

First, we substitute [MATH: A(-1,3)] into the equation: [MATH: y|= − 2x + 1; (3)|= − 2(− 1) + 1; 3|= 3✓]

The result is a true statement, so [MATH: A(-1,3)] is a solution to the equation.

Next, we substitute [MATH: B(2,-4)] into the equation: [MATH: y|= − 2x + 1; (− 4)|= − 2(2) + 1; − 4|= − 4 + 1; − 4|= − 3×]

The result is a false statement, so [MATH: B(2,-4)] is not solution to the equation.

Therefore, only [MATH: A(-1,3)] is a solution to the equation.
